subject: math
title: Grade 4 Bar Graphs and Pictographs
seo_title: Grade 4 Bar Graphs and Pictographs Worksheets: Free Math Practice with Answer Key (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: One-to-one correspondence and many-to-one correspondence, using bar graphs and pictographs
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 math worksheets on bar graphs and pictographs for the BC curriculum: keys where 1 symbol = 2, 5 or 10, half symbols, scales of 2, 5 and 10, comparing and totalling data, and choosing a key or scale. 100 questions with an answer key, good FSA numeracy practice.
key_big: Read the key or the scale first. If 1 symbol = 10, then 4 symbols = 40 and half a symbol = 5.
key_sub: On a bar graph, check what the scale counts by. A bar halfway between 40 and 50 shows 45, not 41. Multiply by the key: never read a symbol or a grid space as 1.
body_html:
One-to-one and many-to-one

In a pictograph, each symbol stands for a number. If 1 symbol = 1 student, that is one-to-one correspondence. If 1 symbol = 2, 5 or 10 students, that is many-to-one. Many-to-one makes big numbers quick to draw: 80 salmon is only 8 symbols when 1 symbol = 10.

Read a pictograph

Look at the key first. Count the symbols by 2s, 5s or 10s. Half a symbol stands for half of the key.

Example

How many students chose soccer?

4 circles. Count by 2s: 2, 4, 6, 8.

Answer: 8 students

Example

How many more sockeye than Chinook?

Sockeye 6 × 10 = 60. Chinook 3 × 10 = 30. 60 − 30 = 30.

Answer: 30 more salmon

Read a bar graph

A good bar graph has a title, labels, a scale and a source. Find what the scale counts by: 2s, 5s or 10s. If a bar ends halfway between two lines, the number is halfway between them.

Example

How many more rainy days were there in November than in February?

November 20. February is halfway between 12 and 14, so 13. 20 − 13 = 7.

Answer: 7 more rainy days

Choose a key or a scale

Look at the data. If every number is in the 5 times table, a key or scale of 5 works. If every number is in the 10 times table, use 10: it needs the fewest symbols or lines. Numbers that end in 5 can use half symbols when the key is 10.

Example

Data: 30, 50, 25, 40 laps. Which key?

25 is not in the 10 times table, but every number is in the 5 times table.

Answer: 1 symbol = 5 laps

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Reading each symbol as 1 (4 circles = 4)Use the key: 4 circles of 10 = 40
Saying half a symbol = 1 for every keyHalf a symbol is half of the key: half of 10 is 5
Leaving out a half symbolAdd it on: 4 and a half stars of 10 = 45
Reading a bar between lines as the lower lineHalfway between 40 and 50 is 45
Counting grid spaces instead of reading the scaleRead the number on the scale

faq.q: What do Grade 4 students learn about graphs in the BC math curriculum?
faq.a: The BC Grade 4 curriculum includes one-to-one and many-to-one correspondence, using bar graphs and pictographs. Students read and make graphs where one symbol or one grid line stands for 2, 5, 10 or more, then compare the data and draw conclusions.

faq.q: What is many-to-one correspondence in a pictograph?
faq.a: It means one symbol stands for more than one thing. If the key says 1 star = 5 students, then 3 stars show 15 students. One-to-one correspondence means 1 symbol = 1 thing.

faq.q: How do you read half a symbol in a pictograph?
faq.a: Half a symbol stands for half of the key. If 1 circle = 10 salmon, half a circle = 5 salmon; if 1 circle = 2 students, half a circle = 1 student.

faq.q: Are bar graphs and pictographs on the Grade 4 FSA?
faq.a: The Grade 4 FSA numeracy section is based on the BC curriculum and can include reading information from graphs and tables to solve problems. Practising with keys and scales, as in these worksheets, is good preparation.

items.q: How many students chose lacrosse?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 2 students. The Lacrosse row has 1 circle: 1 × 2 = 2 students. (1 student would mean each circle is 1.)
Every star stands for the same number, so the row with the most stars shows the most. The Liam row has 7 stars: 7 × 2 = 14 books.

items.q: How many bald eagles were seen?
items.e: Look at the key: each square stands for 2 birds. The Eagle row has 1 square and half a square: 1 × 2 = 2, and half of 2 is 1, so 2 + 1 = 3 birds. (2 birds would mean each square is 1.)

items.q: In this pictograph, what does half a circle stand for?
items.e: The key says one whole circle = 2 books. Half a circle is half of 2, which is 1 book. (Half a symbol is not always 1. It is half of the key.)
Half a star is 1. The Crow row has 6 stars and half a star: 6 × 2 = 12, and half of 2 is 1, so 12 + 1 = 13 birds.

items.q: Each circle stands for 2 students. 16 students chose soccer. How many circles should be in the Soccer row?
items.e: Count by 2s until you reach 16: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16. That is 8 steps, so draw 8 circles. Check: 8 × 2 = 16. (Drawing 16 circles would mean each circle stands for 1.)

items.q: How many laps did the Grade 4 students run?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 5 laps. The Gr. 4 row has 6 circles: 6 × 5 = 30 laps. (6 laps would mean each circle is 1.)
Each star = 5. 15 ÷ 5 = 3, so look for 3 stars. The Bus row has 3 stars: 3 × 5 = 15 students.

items.q: Which row shows the fewest salmon?
items.e: Every square stands for the same number, so the row with the fewest squares shows the fewest. The Chum row has 4 squares: 4 × 5 = 20 salmon.

items.q: Each square stands for 5 salmon. The class counted 35 coho salmon. How many squares should be in the Coho row?
items.e: Count by 5s until you reach 35: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35. That is 7 steps, so draw 7 squares. Check: 7 × 5 = 35. (Drawing 35 squares would mean each square stands for 1.)
Look at the key: each star stands for 5 cans. The Mr. Gill row has 6 stars: 6 × 5 = 30 cans. (6 cans would mean each star is 1.)

items.q: How many squares are in the Thu row?
items.e: Count the symbols in the row: 7 squares. Check with the key: 7 × 5 = 35. (The row does not have 35 squares. That would be the number of visitors.)

items.q: How many students come by car to school?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 10 students. The Car row has 1 circle: 1 × 10 = 10 students. (1 student would mean each circle is 1.)
Look at the key: each star stands for 10 visitors. The Tue row has 2 stars and half a star: 2 × 10 = 20, and half of 10 is 5, so 20 + 5 = 25 visitors. (3 visitors would mean each star is 1.)

items.q: In this pictograph, what does half a square stand for?
items.e: The key says one whole square = 10 salmon. Half a square is half of 10, which is 5 salmon. (Half a symbol is not always 1. It is half of the key.)

items.q: Which row shows 30 laps?
items.e: Each circle = 10. 30 ÷ 10 = 3, so look for 3 circles. The Gr. 7 row has 3 circles: 3 × 10 = 30 laps.
Look at the key: each star stands for 10 cans. The Ms. Lee row has 2 stars and half a star: 2 × 10 = 20, and half of 10 is 5, so 20 + 5 = 25 cans. (3 cans would mean each star is 1.)

items.q: Each star stands for 10 cans. Ms. Ward’s class collected 80 cans for the food bank. How many stars should be in the class’s row?
items.e: Count by 10s until you reach 80: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80. That is 8 steps, so draw 8 stars. Check: 8 × 10 = 80. (Drawing 80 stars would mean each star stands for 1.)

items.q: Which row shows the most visitors?
items.e: Every circle stands for the same number, so the row with the most circles shows the most. The Fri row has 6 circles: 6 × 10 = 60 visitors.
Count the symbols in the row: 2 and a half stars. Check with the key: 2 × 10 + 5 = 25. (The row does not have 25 stars. That would be the number of cans.)

items.q: What does the scale on this bar graph count by?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 2, 4, 6 … Each line is 2 more than the one before, so the scale counts by 2s. (Do not count the lines by 1s.)

items.q: How many ducks were seen?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. The bar for Duck ends on the line for 12. So the answer is 12 birds.

items.q: How many students chose soccer?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. The bar for Soccer ends halfway between 6 and 8, so it shows 7. So the answer is 7 students.

items.q: Which bar shows 9 books?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. Find 9 on the scale. The bar for Liam ends halfway between 8 and 10, so it shows 9.

items.q: Which bar shows the fewest birds?
items.e: The bar for Heron is the shortest one. The bar for Heron ends on the line for 8.

items.q: What does the scale on this bar graph count by?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 5, 10, 15 … Each line is 5 more than the one before, so the scale counts by 5s. (Do not count the lines by 1s.)

items.q: How many sockeye salmon were counted?
items.e: The scale goes up by 5s. The bar for Sockeye ends on the line for 40. So the answer is 40 salmon.

items.q: Which bar shows 10 laps?
items.e: The scale goes up by 5s. Find 10 on the scale. The bar for Gr. 3 ends on the line for 10.

items.q: How many students chose basketball?
items.e: The scale goes up by 5s. The bar for Basketball ends on the line for 15. So the answer is 15 students.

items.q: Which bar shows the most laps?
items.e: The bar for Gr. 4 is the tallest one. The bar for Gr. 4 ends on the line for 25.

items.q: What does the scale on this bar graph count by?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 10, 20, 30 … Each line is 10 more than the one before, so the scale counts by 10s. (Do not count the lines by 1s.)

items.q: How many visitors came on Wednesday?
items.e: The scale goes up by 10s. The bar for Wed ends on the line for 30. So the answer is 30 visitors.

items.q: How many students walk to school?
items.e: The scale goes up by 10s. The bar for Walk ends halfway between 80 and 90, so it shows 85. So the answer is 85 students.

items.q: Which bar shows 85 salmon?
items.e: The scale goes up by 10s. Find 85 on the scale. The bar for Chinook ends halfway between 80 and 90, so it shows 85.

items.q: How many laps did the Grade 6 students run?
items.e: The scale goes up by 10s. The bar for Gr. 6 ends halfway between 30 and 40, so it shows 35. So the answer is 35 laps.

items.q: How many students ride a bike to school?
items.e: The scale goes up by 10s. The bar for Bike ends on the line for 80. So the answer is 80 students.

items.q: Birds seen in Stanley Park: Crow 8, Duck 13, Gull 6, Jay 10. Which bar graph shows this data?
items.e: C matches every number (the scale goes up by 2s). A: two bars are the wrong way round; B: a bar is on the line below (it should be halfway between two lines); D: one bar is one line too high.

items.q: Visitors to the book fair: Mon 40, Tue 65, Wed 30, Thu 50. Which bar graph shows this data?
items.e: A matches every number (the scale goes up by 10s). B: two bars are the wrong way round; C: a bar is on the line below (it should be halfway between two lines); D: one bar is one line too high.

items.q: Which list matches this bar graph? The numbers are in this order: Ms. Lee, Mr. Gill, Ms. Ward, Mr. Chen.
items.e: The scale counts by 10s. The bar for Ms. Lee ends on the line for 40. The bar for Mr. Gill ends on the line for 70. The bar for Ms. Ward ends on the line for 50. The bar for Mr. Chen ends on the line for 60. Counting grid spaces instead of reading the scale gives 4, 7, 5, 6.

items.q: On a bar graph with a scale of 10s, a bar ends halfway between the lines for 40 and 50. What number does the bar show?
items.e: Halfway between 40 and 50 is 45, because 45 is 5 more than 40 and 5 less than 50. (41 would mean halfway is 1 more. Halfway is half of the scale: half of 10 is 5.)

items.q: How many more books did Olivia read than Simran?
items.e: Each circle stands for 2 books. Olivia: 7 × 2 = 14. Simran: 4 × 2 + 1 = 9. How many more means find the difference: 14 − 9 = 5 books.

items.q: How many more students chose basketball than lacrosse?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. Basketball: 13. Lacrosse: 7. How many more means find the difference: 13 − 7 = 6 students. (3 is the difference in grid spaces, not in students.)

items.q: How many more coho salmon than Chinook salmon were counted?
items.e: Each square stands for 5 salmon. Coho: 5 × 5 = 25. Chinook: 1 × 5 = 5. How many more means find the difference: 25 − 5 = 20 salmon. (4 is the difference in symbols, not in salmon.)

items.q: How many more cans did Ms. Lee’s class collect than Mr. Chen’s class?
items.e: The scale goes up by 5s. Ms. Lee: 35. Mr. Chen: 15. How many more means find the difference: 35 − 15 = 20 cans. (4 is the difference in grid spaces, not in cans.)
Each star stands for 10 visitors. Thu: 5 × 10 + 5 = 55. Fri: 2 × 10 = 20. How many more means find the difference: 55 − 20 = 35 visitors.

items.q: How many more students come by car to school than ride a bike?
items.e: The scale goes up by 10s. Car: 90. Bike: 65. How many more means find the difference: 90 − 65 = 25 students.

items.q: How many fewer bald eagles than herons were seen?
items.e: Each circle stands for 2 birds. Heron: 5 × 2 = 10. Eagle: 1 × 2 + 1 = 3. How many fewer means find the difference: 10 − 3 = 7 birds.

items.q: How many fewer visitors came on Friday than on Thursday?
items.e: The scale goes up by 5s. Thu: 30. Fri: 20. How many fewer means find the difference: 30 − 20 = 10 visitors. (2 is the difference in grid spaces, not in visitors.)

items.q: How many fewer Chinook salmon than pink salmon were counted?
items.e: Each square stands for 10 salmon. Pink: 4 × 10 + 5 = 45. Chinook: 1 × 10 = 10. How many fewer means find the difference: 45 − 10 = 35 salmon.

items.q: How many fewer laps did the Grade 5 students run than the Grade 7 students?
items.e: The scale goes up by 10s. Gr. 7: 80. Gr. 5: 45. How many fewer means find the difference: 80 − 45 = 35 laps.
Each star stands for 5 students. Lacrosse: 7 × 5 = 35. Swimming: 3 × 5 = 15. Altogether means add: 35 + 15 = 50 students.

items.q: How many books did Simran and Ethan read altogether?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. Simran: 3. Ethan: 4. Altogether means add: 3 + 4 = 7 books.

items.q: How many cans did Ms. Ward’s class and Mr. Gill’s class collect altogether?
items.e: Each circle stands for 10 cans. Ms. Ward: 6 × 10 = 60. Mr. Gill: 1 × 10 + 5 = 15. Altogether means add: 60 + 15 = 75 cans.

items.q: How many laps did the Grade 4 students and the Grade 7 students run altogether?
items.e: The scale goes up by 10s. Gr. 4: 10. Gr. 7: 55. Altogether means add: 10 + 55 = 65 laps.

items.q: How many birds were seen altogether?
items.e: Each square stands for 2 birds. Read every row: Duck 13, Eagle 12, Crow 11, Heron 4. Add them: 13 + 12 + 11 + 4 = 40 birds. (38 leaves out the half symbols.)

items.q: How many students voted altogether?
items.e: The scale goes up by 5s. Read every bar: Swimming 20, Hockey 15, Lacrosse 30, Basketball 40. Add them: 20 + 15 + 30 + 40 = 105 students. (21 counts grid spaces, not students.)
Each star stands for 5 cans. Read every row: Ms. Ward 25, Ms. Lee 15, Mr. Gill 30, Mr. Chen 35. Add them: 25 + 15 + 30 + 35 = 105 cans. (21 is the number of symbols.)

items.q: How many visitors came altogether?
items.e: The scale goes up by 10s. Read every bar: Tue 60, Wed 85, Thu 90, Fri 10. Add them: 60 + 85 + 90 + 10 = 245 visitors. (240 leaves out the halves between the lines.)

items.q: How many salmon were counted altogether?
items.e: Each circle stands for 10 salmon. Read every row: Pink 60, Sockeye 15, Coho 55, Chinook 25. Add them: 60 + 15 + 55 + 25 = 155 salmon. (140 leaves out the half symbols.)

items.q: How many books did the students read altogether?
items.e: The scale goes up by 2s. Read every bar: Simran 4, Mei 15, Ethan 14, Olivia 13. Add them: 4 + 15 + 14 + 13 = 46 books. (44 leaves out the halves between the lines.)

sets.title: Choose the key or scale and draw conclusions

items.q: Which key shows one-to-one correspondence?
items.e: One-to-one means one symbol for each one thing: 1 symbol = 1 student. The other keys are many-to-one: one symbol stands for many students.

items.q: Mei counted 80 salmon. Why is a key of 1 symbol = 10 salmon better than 1 symbol = 1 salmon?
c: She does not need a key.
items.e: With 1 symbol = 10 salmon, 80 salmon is 80 ÷ 10 = 8 symbols. With 1 symbol = 1 salmon she would draw 80 symbols. The number of salmon stays 80 either way, and the key is still needed.

items.q: Owen will make a bar graph of this data: 20, 45, 30, 35. He wants every bar to end on a line, with as few lines as possible. Which scale should he use?
items.e: All the numbers are in the 5 times table, so with a scale of 5s every bar ends on a line, up to 45 (9 lines). A scale of 1s needs 45 lines. With 2s or 10s, 45 and 35 do not end on a line.

items.q: Owen will make a bar graph of this data: 60, 90, 40, 80. He wants every bar to end on a line, with as few lines as possible. Which scale should he use?
items.e: All the numbers are in the 10 times table, so a scale of 10s works with only 9 lines up to 90. 5s also works but needs 18 lines, and 2s needs 45 lines. With 100s, no bar ends on a line.

items.q: Owen will make a bar graph of this data: 8, 14, 6, 12. He wants every bar to end on a line, with as few lines as possible. Which scale should he use?
items.e: All the numbers are even, so with a scale of 2s every bar ends on a line, up to 14 (7 lines). 1s needs 14 lines. With 5s or 10s, 8, 14, 6 and 12 do not end on a line.

items.q: Hana will make a pictograph of this data: 30, 50, 25, 40 laps. She wants only whole symbols, and as few symbols as possible. Which key should she use?
items.e: Every number is in the 5 times table, so 1 symbol = 5 laps gives whole symbols: 30 ÷ 5 = 6, 50 ÷ 5 = 10, 25 ÷ 5 = 5, 40 ÷ 5 = 8. A key of 1 also gives whole symbols, but more of them. A key of 2 does not work for 25.

items.q: Hana will make a pictograph of this data: 12, 8, 16, 10 books. She wants only whole symbols, and as few symbols as possible. Which key should she use?
items.e: Every number is in the 2 times table, so 1 symbol = 2 books gives whole symbols: 12 ÷ 2 = 6, 8 ÷ 2 = 4, 16 ÷ 2 = 8, 10 ÷ 2 = 5. A key of 1 also gives whole symbols, but more of them. A key of 5 does not work for 12.

items.q: Hana will make a pictograph of this data: 70, 40, 90, 60 cans. She wants only whole symbols, and as few symbols as possible. Which key should she use?
items.e: Every number is in the 10 times table, so 1 symbol = 10 cans gives whole symbols: 70 ÷ 10 = 7, 40 ÷ 10 = 4, 90 ÷ 10 = 9, 60 ÷ 10 = 6. A key of 2 or 5 also gives whole symbols, but more of them. A key of 20 does not work for 70.

items.q: In a pictograph, each star stands for 10 laps. The Grade 4 students ran 45 laps at the Terry Fox Run. How should their row look?
items.e: 45 = 40 + 5. 40 laps is 4 stars (4 × 10). 5 is half of 10, so add half a star: 4 and a half stars.

items.q: In a pictograph, each circle stands for 2 bald eagles. Kai saw 7 eagles. How should his row look?
items.e: 7 = 6 + 1. 6 eagles is 3 circles (3 × 2). 1 is half of 2, so add half a circle: 3 and a half circles.

items.q: In Liam’s pictograph, each circle = 5 students, and the Soccer row has 6 circles. He makes a new pictograph where each circle = 10 students. How many circles go in the Soccer row now?
items.e: First find the number of students: 6 × 5 = 30. Then use the new key: 30 ÷ 10 = 3 circles. A bigger key means fewer symbols. (12 circles doubles the symbols instead of halving them.)

items.q: In Ava’s pictograph, each star = 2 books, and her row has 10 stars. She makes a new pictograph where each star = 5 books. How many stars go in her row now?
items.e: First find the number of books: 10 × 2 = 20. Then use the new key: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 stars. (2 stars comes from 10 ÷ 5, which forgets that each old star was 2 books.)

items.q: Every bar graph needs a title, labels, a scale and a source. What is missing from this bar graph?
items.e: The graph has a scale (0, 10, 20 …), labels (Class and Cans) and a source under the graph. It has no title at the top. A good title is “Cans for the food bank”.

items.q: Which list matches this pictograph? The numbers are in this order: Chinook, Coho, Sockeye, Pink.
items.e: Each square = 5 salmon. Chinook 4 × 5 = 20, Coho 7 × 5 = 35, Sockeye 3 × 5 = 15, Pink 6 × 5 = 30. (4, 7, 3, 6 counts the squares as 1 each, and 40, 70, 30, 60 uses a key of 10 by mistake.)

items.q: Which statement is true?
c: Hockey got more votes than swimming.
Soccer got twice as many votes as hockey.
Swimming got 1 more vote than hockey.
items.e: The scale counts by 2s. Swimming 6, hockey 5 (halfway between 4 and 6): 6 − 5 = 1, so this is true. Lacrosse (2) got the fewest votes. Twice hockey would be 10, but soccer got 9.

items.q: Which sports did fewer than 5 students choose?
items.e: Lacrosse ends on 2. Basketball ends halfway between 2 and 4, so 3. Both are less than 5. Hockey ends halfway between 4 and 6, so it is 5, and 5 is not fewer than 5. (Reading hockey as 4 adds hockey by mistake.)

items.q: Ava says, “Soccer is the favourite sport of every Grade 4 student in BC.” Is she right?
c: Yes. Soccer has the tallest bar.
No. The data is from one class only.
No. Swimming has the tallest bar.
items.e: The source says the data is from one Grade 4 class vote. It tells us about this class, not every student in BC. Even in this class, most students did not choose soccer: 9 out of 25.

items.q: Two bar graphs show the same salmon count. Graph A has a scale of 10s, and its Coho bar ends halfway between 30 and 40. Graph B has a scale of 5s. Where does the Coho bar end on Graph B?
items.e: Halfway between 30 and 40 is 35. Graph B counts by 5s, so it has a line for 35. The bar ends right on that line.

items.q: Which statement is true?
c: Grade 5 ran more laps than Grade 4.
Grade 6 ran twice as many laps as Grade 3.
Grade 4 and Grade 5 ran the same number of laps.
items.e: The scale counts by 10s. Grade 3 ends halfway between 30 and 40, so 35. Grade 6 ends on 70. 35 × 2 = 70, so Grade 6 ran twice as many. Grade 7 is 85, not 80, and Grade 5 (40) ran fewer than Grade 4 (50).

items.q: The number of salmon goes up the same way each day. If it keeps going, how many salmon will the class count on Friday?
items.e: 20, 30, 40, 50: each bar is 10 more than the day before. 50 + 10 = 60 salmon on Friday. (6 counts grid spaces, not salmon.)

sets.title: Word problems: sports, salmon and rainy days

items.q: How many students chose lacrosse?
items.e: The scale counts by 5s. The lacrosse bar ends on the line for 15. (3 counts the grid spaces as 1 each.)

items.q: Which month had the most rainy days?
items.e: The tallest bar is November. It ends on the line for 20. December is 19, just below it.

items.q: How many circles are in the Coho row?
items.e: The Coho row has 4 whole circles and half a circle. That shows 45 salmon, but it is only 4 and a half circles.

items.q: How many more students chose soccer than lacrosse?
items.e: Soccer 35, lacrosse 15. How many more means subtract: 35 − 15 = 20. (4 is the difference in grid spaces, and 50 adds the two bars.)

items.q: How many rainy days were there in January?
items.e: The scale counts by 2s. The January bar ends halfway between 16 and 18, so it shows 17. (16 and 18 read the line below or above. 19 is December.)

items.q: How many coho salmon were counted?
items.e: Each circle = 10 salmon, so half a circle = 5. The Coho row has 4 circles and half a circle: 4 × 10 = 40, and half of 10 is 5, so 40 + 5 = 45 salmon. (5 reads each circle as 1. 41 reads the half circle as 1.)

items.q: The school will start clubs for the two most popular sports. Which two?
items.e: The two tallest bars are soccer (35) and basketball (30). Hockey is 25, the third tallest.

items.q: How many more rainy days were there in November than in February?
items.e: November 20. February ends halfway between 12 and 14, so 13. 20 − 13 = 7. (Reading February as 12 gives 8; as 14 gives 6.)

items.q: Simran keeps a log of rainy days in Vancouver. She counted 60 rainy days. In her pictograph, each cloud stands for 5 days. How many clouds does she draw?
items.e: 60 ÷ 5 = 12, so 12 clouds. Check by counting by 5s twelve times: 5, 10, … 60. (6 clouds would be right for a key of 10.)

items.q: Mei went whale watching near Victoria. In her pictograph, each symbol stands for 2 orcas. Her Saturday row has 4 and a half symbols. How many orcas did she see on Saturday?
items.e: 4 symbols × 2 = 8 orcas. Half a symbol is half of 2, which is 1. 8 + 1 = 9 orcas. (8 leaves out the half symbol, and 10 reads it as a whole one.)

items.q: The students who chose basketball make teams of 5 for a lunch tournament. How many teams do they make?
items.e: Basketball ends on 30. 30 ÷ 5 = 6 teams. (7 teams comes from using the soccer bar, 35. 150 multiplies instead of dividing.)

items.q: That February had 28 days. How many days in February were not rainy?
items.e: February had 13 rainy days. 28 − 13 = 15 days without rain. (13 is the rainy days, 16 reads February as 12, and 41 adds.)

items.q: How many more sockeye than Chinook salmon were counted?
items.e: Sockeye: 7 × 10 = 70. Chinook: 2 × 10 + 5 = 25. 70 − 25 = 45. (50 leaves out the half circle; 40 reads it as a whole circle; 95 adds.)

items.q: The pink salmon were counted over 3 days, with the same number each day. How many pink salmon were counted each day?
items.e: Pink: 6 circles × 10 = 60 salmon. 60 ÷ 3 = 20 each day. (2 divides the 6 circles, not the salmon; 180 multiplies.)

items.q: Which statement is true?
c: January had more rainy days than December.
Every month had more than 15 rainy days.
March had the fewest rainy days.
December had 3 more rainy days than March.
items.e: December 19 and March 16: 19 − 16 = 3, so this is true. January (17) had fewer than December (19). February (13) had the fewest, so not every month had more than 15.

items.q: Every student chose one sport. How many students took part in the survey?
Owen’s class voted: 18 students chose soccer and 14 chose hockey. In his pictograph, each ball stands for 2 votes. How many more balls are in the Soccer row than in the Hockey row?
items.e: Soccer: 18 ÷ 2 = 9 balls. Hockey: 14 ÷ 2 = 7 balls. 9 − 7 = 2 balls. (4 is the difference in votes, not in balls.)

items.q: How many salmon were counted altogether?
items.e: Chinook 25, Coho 45, Sockeye 70, Pink 60, Chum 35. 25 + 45 + 70 + 60 + 35 = 235. (25 counts the circles; 220 leaves out the three half circles.)

items.q: How many rainy days were there altogether from November to March?
items.e: Read every bar: 20, 19, 17, 13 and 16. 20 + 19 + 17 + 13 + 16 = 85. (82 reads the three bars between lines on the line below; 69 forgets March.)

items.q: On a bar graph with a scale of 10s, the Grade 4 bar for the Terry Fox Run ends halfway between 60 and 70. The Grade 5 bar ends on 80. How many more laps did Grade 5 run than Grade 4?
items.e: Grade 4: halfway between 60 and 70 is 65. 80 − 65 = 15 laps. (Reading Grade 4 as 60 gives 20; as 70 gives 10.)
